analogy.p: Imagine each gene is a recipe and you inherit two recipe cards, one from each parent. If one card says 'make a normal dish' (dominant F) and the other says 'make a faulty dish' (recessive f), the kitchen follows the normal card, so you are healthy, but you can still hand your faulty card to a child (a carrier). Only if both cards are faulty does the kitchen produce the faulty dish (CF). For polydactyly, the faulty card is the bossy one: if even one is present it is followed. This analogy breaks down because real alleles do not 'read' cards; the dominant allele makes a working protein whose effect hides the effect of the recessive allele, and the process in cells is chemical, not a choice.
analogy.t: Alleles as a pair of recipe cards

bullets: **Alleles** are different versions of the same gene, found at the same position (locus) on a pair of chromosomes. Having two alleles for each gene is why dominant and recessive inheritance exists.
**22 of the 23 pairs** are called **autosomes**. They carry genes for general body characteristics and look the same in males and females.
**The 23rd pair** are the **sex chromosomes**. They are the only pair that differs between males and females, and they carry the genes that determine biological sex.
**Gametes** (sperm and egg) are made by **meiosis**, which halves the chromosome number, so each gamete has **23 single chromosomes**, one from each pair. Fertilisation restores 46.
The **genome** is the entire genetic material of an organism. The Human Genome Project mapped the whole human genome, which helps scientists find alleles linked to inherited disorders.

**Phenotype** is the characteristic you can see or measure; **genotype** is the combination of alleles you have. Disorders are described at both levels: for example the genotype ff gives the phenotype of cystic fibrosis.
Link to other topics: this builds directly on meiosis, DNA structure and genetic inheritance (Punnett squares) earlier in section 4.6.
core.h: Chromosomes and the genome: setting the scene
core.p: The nucleus of a human body cell contains **23 pairs of chromosomes**, which is **46 chromosomes** in total. Each chromosome is a long, coiled molecule of **DNA** that carries many **genes**. A gene is a small section of DNA that codes for a particular **protein**, so the genes you inherit decide the proteins your cells can make, and therefore many of your characteristics. One chromosome in each pair came from your mother's egg and the other from your father's sperm, so you carry **two alleles** (versions) of every gene.

bullets: **Female = XX; male = XY.** Learn this exactly: examiners ask you to label genotypes in a cross.
**All eggs carry an X chromosome**, because the mother's cells only contain X chromosomes and meiosis separates the pair so each egg gets one X.
**Half the sperm carry an X and half carry a Y**, because meiosis separates the X and Y of the father into different sperm cells.
If an **X-carrying sperm** fertilises the egg, the zygote is **XX** and develops as a **girl**. If a **Y-carrying sperm** fertilises the egg, the zygote is **XY** and develops as a **boy**.
The Y chromosome is **much smaller** than the X chromosome and carries far fewer genes. The X chromosome carries many genes unrelated to sex.
Sex is therefore decided at the moment of **fertilisation**, by chance, depending on which sperm reaches the egg first.
Do not say the mother 'decides' or that the egg has a Y chromosome; the **egg never contains a Y**.
core.p: In the 23rd pair, **females have two X chromosomes (XX)** and **males have one X and one shorter Y chromosome (XY)**. The Y chromosome carries a gene that triggers the embryo to develop **testes**, so whether a baby is male or female depends on whether the sperm that fertilised the egg carried an X or a Y. The mother can only pass on an X, because both of her sex chromosomes are X. The father can pass on either an X or a Y, so **it is the father's sperm that determines the sex of the child**.

bullets: Step 1: state the parent genotypes (mother XX, father XY).
Step 2: circle the gametes: mother X and X; father X and Y. Each gamete has **one** sex chromosome.
Step 3: fill the grid: XX, XY, XX, XY.
Step 4: state the result as a ratio, fraction, percentage or probability, and say which genotype is which sex.
**Probability, not a guarantee.** A 1:1 ratio does not mean a family of 4 will have exactly 2 boys and 2 girls. It means each fertilisation has a 50% chance of each sex.
**Each birth is independent.** Having had three girls does not make a boy more likely next time; the chance is still 1 in 2, because the sperm that fertilises the egg is a fresh random event.
Over a very large population the numbers of males and females born are very close to equal, which is the expected result of a 1:1 ratio.
Probabilities are multiplied for independent events: the chance of two girls in a row is 1/2 x 1/2 = **1/4**.
core.h: Using a Punnett square to show sex inheritance
core.p: A **genetic cross diagram** (Punnett square) is a grid that shows every possible combination of gametes. To show how sex is inherited you write the parental genotypes (**XX** for the mother, **XY** for the father), list the gametes each can make along the top and side of the grid, and fill in the four boxes by combining one allele from each side. Two boxes show **XX (female)** and two show **XY (male)**, so the probability of a girl is **2/4 = 1/2 = 50%** and of a boy is also **50%**, a **1:1 ratio**.

bullets: The disorder is caused by the **genotype**, so it can be predicted using a genetic cross, but each fertilisation is random so only **probabilities** can be given.
**Dominant allele:** shown in the phenotype even if only **one copy** is present (genotypes DD or Dd). It is written with a **capital letter**.
**Recessive allele:** only shown in the phenotype when **two copies** are present (genotype dd or ff). It is written with a **lower-case letter**.
**Homozygous** = two identical alleles (DD or dd). **Heterozygous** = two different alleles (Dd).
A person with one dominant and one recessive allele shows the **dominant** characteristic.
Not all inherited disorders follow this simple one-gene pattern, but at GCSE you only need these two examples and the rules above.
Link to other topics: the faulty allele is originally produced by a **mutation** (see Variation and mutation) and persists because of how alleles are passed down.
core.p: An **inherited disorder** is a medical condition caused by a **faulty allele** that is passed from parent to child in the gametes. Some inherited disorders are caused by a **dominant** allele, which only needs one copy to have an effect, and others by a **recessive** allele, which only has an effect when a person has **two copies**. You need to know one example of each: **polydactyly** (dominant) and **cystic fibrosis** (recessive). In both cases the faulty allele arose originally from a **mutation**, then stayed in the population because it was copied and inherited.

bullets: **Dominant allele (D)** causes the condition, so polydactyly can appear in **every generation** if a parent is affected.

An **unaffected person must be dd**: they cannot carry the allele without showing it, because it is dominant. Two unaffected parents (dd x dd) can therefore **never** have an affected child (unless a new mutation occurs).
**Dd x dd (one affected, heterozygous parent):** gametes D, d and d, d give Dd, Dd, dd, dd, so **50% (1 in 2)** of the children are expected to have polydactyly.
**DD x dd:** every child is Dd, so **100%** are affected, although the parent is homozygous.
**Dd x Dd:** the grid gives DD, Dd, Dd, dd, so **75% (3 in 4)** are affected and **25%** are unaffected, a **3:1** ratio.
Because the allele is dominant it is **not hidden** and there are **no carriers**: anyone who has the allele has the condition.
Common error: the condition is called a 'disorder' but it is **not** the more common phenotype; that does not change the fact that it is dominant. Dominant does not mean 'most common' or 'strongest'.
core.p: **Polydactyly** is an inherited condition in which a baby is born with **extra fingers or toes** on one or more hands or feet. It is caused by a **dominant allele**, so a person only needs to inherit **one copy** of the allele from one parent to be affected. The allele is shown here as **D** (polydactyly) and the normal allele as **d**. People with genotype **DD or Dd** have extra digits and people with **dd** have a normal number of fingers and toes. Polydactyly is usually not life-threatening, and the extra digits can often be removed by minor surgery.

bullets: The faulty allele makes a faulty membrane protein, so the cell membranes do not work normally. The mucus becomes thick and sticky rather than thin and runny.
In the **lungs** the sticky mucus traps bacteria, so people with CF get frequent serious lung infections and have trouble breathing.
In the **digestive system** the thick mucus can block tubes that carry digestive enzymes to the gut, so digesting and absorbing food is harder.
A **carrier** has the genotype **Ff**. Carriers are healthy but can pass the allele on to their children.

**Ff x Ff (two carriers):** gametes F, f and F, f give FF, Ff, Ff, ff. The probability of a child with CF is **1/4 = 25%**, a carrier child is **50%** and an unaffected non-carrier is **25%**. The phenotype ratio is **3 unaffected : 1 CF**.
**Ff x FF:** no child can have CF (FF, FF, Ff, Ff), but 50% are carriers.
**Ff x ff:** FF cannot occur; the children are Ff, Ff, ff, ff so **50%** have CF and 50% are carriers.
**ff x ff:** all children have CF (100%).
Carriers cannot tell they carry the allele without a genetic test, so two healthy parents can be surprised by a child with CF.
core.h: Cystic fibrosis: a recessive inherited disorder
core.p: **Cystic fibrosis (CF)** is a disorder of the **cell membranes**. A person with CF produces **thick, sticky mucus** in the airways and gut, which causes breathing difficulties, repeated chest infections and problems digesting food. It is caused by a **recessive allele**, shown as **f**, and the normal dominant allele is **F**. Only people with genotype **ff** have cystic fibrosis. People with **FF** are unaffected and people with **Ff** are unaffected **carriers**: they have one copy of the faulty allele but also a working dominant allele, so they show no symptoms.

bullets: Each carrier parent has a **1 in 2 chance** of passing on f in each gamete; the child needs f from both, giving 1/2 x 1/2 = **1/4**.
If both parents are **unaffected** but a child has a **recessive** disorder, the parents must both be **carriers (Ff)**. This is a favourite examiner deduction.
If both parents have the **same dominant condition** and a child does **not**, both parents must be **heterozygous (Dd)**, because the child must be dd and has received one d from each.
Recessive harmful alleles can stay in a population because carriers are healthy and still reproduce, so the allele is passed on without being removed by natural selection.
Each pregnancy is independent: having one child with CF does **not** mean the next three will be fine. The risk is 1 in 4 **every** time.
Link to other topics: this helps explain why harmful recessive alleles remain in a population (natural selection and evolution).
core.h: Why recessive disorders can skip generations
core.p: Because carriers show no symptoms, a recessive allele can be passed down through many generations without anyone being affected. A disorder appears only when **two carriers have children** and the child inherits the faulty allele from **both** parents. This is why cystic fibrosis often seems to appear 'out of nowhere' in families with no history of the disorder, whereas a dominant disorder like polydactyly usually has an affected parent.

bullets: **Two unaffected parents with an affected child** means the disorder is **recessive**, and both parents are **carriers**. The reasoning is: if it were dominant, an unaffected parent would have to be dd and could not pass on D.
**An affected child must have received an allele from each parent.** If the child is ff, each parent must have at least one f.
**Unaffected individuals in a recessive disorder** are FF or Ff. You often cannot tell which unless their parents or children give you more information, so write 'F_' or 'FF or Ff'.
In a **dominant** disorder, anyone who is unaffected is dd; an affected person with an unaffected parent must be Dd.
State your **reasoning** in the answer: for example 'both parents are unaffected but have an affected child, so they must both carry the recessive allele (Ff), and the child must be ff'.
After finding genotypes, you can draw a Punnett square for any couple in the tree to find the probability of a future child being affected.
Be careful to answer for the **correct generation** and person; examiners often ask about a couple's next child, not the child already born.
core.p: A **family tree** shows how a characteristic or disorder is inherited through the generations. Squares usually show males and circles show females, a horizontal line joins parents, and vertical lines go down to their children. Affected individuals are shaded. To answer questions, work out whether the allele is dominant or recessive by looking for the key pattern, then assign genotypes to individuals one at a time, checking that every parent-child combination is possible.

bullets: IVF involves collecting eggs, fertilising them outside the body, and placing an embryo into the mother's **uterus (womb)**.
Taking a few cells from an early embryo does not usually stop it from developing normally, because early embryo cells are **unspecialised**.
Screening can identify embryos with a **dominant** disorder, a **homozygous recessive** disorder, or those that are **carriers**.
Embryos found to carry the disorder are normally **not implanted** and are discarded (or, in some cases, may be used in research under strict regulations).
It is especially useful for couples who know they are carriers, because without screening each pregnancy has a 1 in 4 chance of a child with CF.
Screening can only detect disorders that scientists know how to test for; it **cannot guarantee a healthy baby**.
Link to other topics: relies on understanding of alleles, inheritance and probability from Punnett squares.
core.p: **Embryo screening** is a process used with **IVF (in vitro fertilisation)**. Eggs are fertilised by sperm in a laboratory and the embryos are allowed to develop for a short time. **One or two cells are removed from each embryo** and their DNA is tested for particular **faulty alleles**, for example the allele for cystic fibrosis. Only embryos without the faulty allele (or embryos chosen by the parents according to the rules) are then placed in the mother's womb. The aim is to **avoid a child being born with a serious inherited disorder**.

bullets: **For (benefits):** it can **prevent suffering** by avoiding children born with serious, painful or life-limiting disorders such as cystic fibrosis.
**For:** it reduces the **emotional strain on families** and the risk of a later termination of pregnancy because a disorder is found in the womb.
**For (economic):** fewer people with serious disorders can mean lower long-term costs of medical care, drugs and support for the NHS and families.
**Against (ethical):** it involves **creating and then destroying embryos**, and some people believe an embryo is a **human life with the right to life** from fertilisation.

**Against (ethical/social):** the **'slippery slope' or 'designer babies' concern**: if we can screen out disorders, people may begin choosing other characteristics such as sex, eye colour or intelligence.
**Against (social):** it may suggest that people living with a disorder are **less valuable** and could increase **discrimination** against disabled people.
**Against (economic):** IVF and screening are **expensive**, so they may not be available to everyone, and money spent could be used elsewhere.
**Against (practical):** IVF is **not always successful**, can be physically and emotionally stressful, and screening cannot test for all disorders so the baby could still have another problem.
A good answer states a view only after weighing both sides and linking each point to a real consequence, using words such as 'however' and 'on the other hand'.
core.h: Economic, social and ethical issues of embryo screening
core.p: AQA expects you to make an **informed judgement** about embryo screening using arguments from different viewpoints. The key is to give **balanced, specific points** and not just say it is 'good' or 'bad'. Arguments are normally grouped into **economic** (to do with money), **social** (to do with society and relationships) and **ethical** (to do with right and wrong).

bullets: Probability of a **girl** = 1/2 (50%). Probability of a child with CF from two carriers = 1/4 (25%).
Probability of a **girl with CF** = 1/2 x 1/4 = **1/8** (12.5%). Probability of a **boy with CF** is also 1/8.
Probability of **two children both with CF** from carrier parents = 1/4 x 1/4 = **1/16**.
Probability that a child is **not** affected by CF = 1 - 1/4 = **3/4** (75%). Use '1 minus' when it is easier to find the chance of the opposite.
Probability of a child being a **carrier** = 2/4 = **1/2**.

If asked about the probability that an **unaffected child** (known not to have CF) is a carrier, the possible genotypes are only FF, Ff, Ff, so the probability is **2/3**. Read the question carefully for this kind of condition.
Show the Punnett square, then the multiplication, and give the final answer in the form requested.
core.p: Higher-tier questions often combine inheritance of a disorder with another event, such as the sex of the baby. Because the events are **independent**, you **multiply the probabilities**. First work out each probability separately using a Punnett square, then multiply. Always give the answer as a fraction, decimal, ratio or percentage as the question asks, and show the working.

bullets: Always **define your letters** and choose one letter for each gene, with the capital for dominant and the lower case for recessive.
Write **gametes in circles** or clearly labelled so the examiner can see each parent's gametes.
Check each box of the grid by writing the **capital letter first** (Ff, not fF), because mark schemes use this convention.
State the answer in the form requested: 'ratio 3:1', '25%', or '1 in 4'.
With a **table of family data**, count the affected individuals and look at whether both parents were affected.
Use **command words** correctly: 'Describe' = give features; 'Explain' = give reasons using 'because'; 'Evaluate' = weigh up and reach a judgement.
core.h: Common examination contexts and data skills
core.p: Questions on this topic usually give a short passage (about a family, the allele, or a screening clinic) and ask you to **draw a cross, state genotypes, give a probability, interpret a family tree, or evaluate screening**. Many marks are for correct use of **allele letters** and for stating that the result is a **probability**. You are expected to define letters at the start (for example, 'F = normal allele, f = CF allele') if the question does not give them.

bullets: **Meiosis**: explains how the chromosome pairs separate into gametes, which is why each gamete has one sex chromosome and one allele per gene.
**Variation and mutation**: new alleles, including the alleles for CF and polydactyly, originally arise by mutation.
**Natural selection**: harmful dominant alleles tend to be removed from a population faster than harmful recessive alleles, because carriers of recessive alleles are healthy and can still reproduce.
**Genetic engineering and gene technology**: scientists research ways to treat inherited disorders by altering genes.
**Gas exchange and digestion**: thick mucus affects how well the lungs and gut work, helping you explain the symptoms of CF.
**Ethics in biology**: the same type of balanced argument is used for cloning, genetic engineering and stem cells.
core.p: This topic ties together several other parts of AQA Biology. The same Punnett square method is used for any single-gene characteristic. The origin of alleles is explained by mutations, the way alleles spread is linked to natural selection, and the effect of CF on cell membranes links back to cell transport and the structure of the gas exchange and digestive systems.

exam: **1 mark** recall: 'State the sex chromosomes of a human female' = XX; 'Name the type of allele that causes polydactyly' = dominant.
**2 marks**: 'Explain why a person with the genotype Ff does not have cystic fibrosis' = F is dominant (1) so the person has a working allele that masks the effect of the recessive allele f (1).

**Genetic cross questions (usually 3 to 4 marks)**: mark scheme points are correct parent genotypes, correct gametes, correct offspring genotypes in the grid, and the correct probability or ratio. Always show all four steps.
Define your **allele letters** (for example, F and f) when you are not told them, and use one letter with capital and lower case; never use letters that look similar when written (like S and s).

'**Explain why** two unaffected parents had a child with CF' = both parents are carriers (heterozygous, Ff) (1); each passes on the recessive allele f in their gamete (1); the child receives two copies (ff) (1).
For **family trees**, point to evidence on the diagram: quote which individuals are affected and which parents are unaffected, then state the genotype reasoning.

**'Calculate the probability'**: give the answer in the form asked (fraction, percentage, ratio) and show the working by writing the Punnett square; 1 mark is often for the correct method even if the final answer is wrong.

**Embryo screening 4 to 6 mark evaluation**: include at least two arguments for and two against, using the terms economic, social and ethical, then give a justified conclusion; do not just list points without explanation.

Use model phrases: 'the allele is recessive so it is only expressed when two copies are present', 'the probability of each child is independent', 'the father's sperm carries either an X or a Y chromosome'.
Be careful with **'describe' versus 'explain'** for CF: describing symptoms (sticky mucus, breathing difficulty) is a different mark point from explaining the genetics.
Check your Punnett square by confirming that the offspring probabilities add up to 4/4 (100%).

mistakes.r: All eggs carry an X chromosome; the sperm carries either X or Y, so the father's sperm decides the sex.
mistakes.w: The mother's egg decides whether the baby is a boy or a girl.

mistakes.r: The 1:1 ratio is a probability; each fertilisation is independent with a 50% chance of each sex.
mistakes.w: Families always have equal numbers of boys and girls, or after three girls a boy is due.

mistakes.r: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele (f); a person must inherit two copies (ff) to have it.
mistakes.w: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a dominant allele.

mistakes.r: Polydactyly is caused by a dominant allele (D); dominant does not mean common.
mistakes.w: Polydactyly is caused by a recessive allele because it is rare.

mistakes.r: A carrier (Ff) has one recessive allele but does not have the disorder because the dominant allele is also present.
mistakes.w: Carriers have cystic fibrosis but with milder symptoms.

mistakes.r: If both parents are carriers (Ff), there is a 1 in 4 (25%) chance of a child with CF.
mistakes.w: Two parents who do not have CF cannot have a child with CF.

mistakes.r: CF is an inherited disorder of cell membranes causing thick sticky mucus, mainly affecting the lungs and digestive system; it is not caused by a pathogen.
mistakes.w: Cystic fibrosis is a disorder of the lungs only, caused by an infection.

mistakes.r: Screening only identifies embryos with the faulty allele so that unaffected embryos can be selected; it does not treat or change genes.
It is a probability for each pregnancy; it does not mean exactly one in four children will be affected.
mistakes.w: A 25% chance means that one in every four children will definitely have the disorder.

mistakes.r: Give balanced, specific arguments (economic, social, ethical) from both sides before reaching a judgement.
mistakes.w: Giving only one side of the argument about embryo screening, or just saying it is wrong.

summary: AQA wants you to know that human body cells have 23 pairs of chromosomes, 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes (XX female, XY male), and to use a genetic cross to show the 1:1 chance of a boy or girl. You must also describe polydactyly (dominant allele) and cystic fibrosis (recessive allele), predict and interpret their inheritance with Punnett squares and family trees, and discuss the economic, social and ethical issues of embryo screening. It matters because inheritance crosses and ethics questions are reliable multi-mark questions on Paper 2.

terms.d: A different version of the same gene.
A small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a particular protein.
A coiled structure of DNA found in the nucleus that carries many genes.
One of the 22 pairs of human chromosomes that are not the sex chromosomes.
The pair of chromosomes that determines sex: XX in females and XY in males.
A sex cell (sperm or egg) with half the usual number of chromosomes, produced by meiosis.
An allele that is shown in the phenotype when it is present on one or both chromosomes.
An allele that is only shown in the phenotype when two copies are present.
Having two identical alleles for a gene, such as DD or dd.
Having two different alleles for a gene, such as Dd.
The combination of alleles a person has for a gene.
The characteristic that is shown, as a result of the genotype and the environment.
A person who has one copy of a recessive allele for a disorder but does not show the disorder.
A medical condition caused by a faulty allele passed on from parents to offspring.
An inherited condition of having extra fingers or toes, caused by a dominant allele.
An inherited disorder of the cell membranes, caused by a recessive allele, that produces thick sticky mucus.
Testing cells from embryos made by IVF for faulty alleles before an embryo is placed in the womb.
In vitro fertilisation: eggs are fertilised by sperm in a laboratory and an embryo is placed in the womb.
A genetic cross diagram that shows all possible combinations of gametes and the resulting offspring genotypes.

worked.ans: The probability is 1/4 (25%, or a 1 in 4 chance). Genotypes FF : Ff : ff = 1 : 2 : 1, phenotype ratio 3 unaffected : 1 with CF (1 mark).
worked.q: Two parents are both carriers of the cystic fibrosis allele. The normal allele is F and the CF allele is f. Draw a genetic cross and calculate the probability that their first child has cystic fibrosis. (4 marks)
steps: Gametes: each parent can produce F or f (1 mark).
Punnett square: FF, Ff, Ff, ff (1 mark).
Only ff has cystic fibrosis: 1 box out of 4.

worked.q: A man with polydactyly (genotype Dd) and a woman without polydactyly have a child. Calculate the chance that the child is a girl with polydactyly. (3 marks)
steps: The woman has no polydactyly, so she must be dd because the allele is dominant.
Cross Dd x dd: Dd, Dd, dd, dd so the probability of polydactyly = 2/4 = 1/2.
Events are independent so multiply: 1/2 x 1/2.

worked.ans: Embryo screening tests cells from embryos made by IVF for the faulty allele so that only an embryo without cystic fibrosis is placed in the womb. This could prevent a child suffering from the thick sticky mucus that causes lung infections and breathing problems, and it spares the family the stress of a child with a serious illness. It could also reduce the long-term medical costs to the NHS. However, embryos that are not chosen are destroyed, and some people believe that an embryo is a human life, so this is ethically wrong. There is also a concern that it could lead to 'designer babies' if other characteristics were selected, and it could suggest that people with disorders are less valuable. IVF is expensive and does not always work, and screening cannot test for every disorder. Overall, I think screening is justified for serious disorders such as cystic fibrosis if it is strictly regulated, because the suffering prevented is great, but there must be limits to stop it being used to choose non-medical characteristics.
